source.title: Consistency for Large Neural Networks: Regression and Classification

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations and formatting are garbled in the extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own neural-network size sweep using MISE and a theoretical prediction-error bound for large regularized networks. These bear on model-wise error behavior, but the paper does not reproduce the original experimental recipe or locate the interpolation threshold.
record.gate_note: The paper's Figure 1 simulation and its model-width prediction-error result bear on model-wise error behavior. The authors also state that different regularization levels can yield double descent or other patterns. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows. The empirical fit/interpolation threshold is not reported; the regression, robust-regression, quantile, classification, and random-forest results do not separately report a double-descent curve.
record.test_reason: Mainly a consistency theory paper. Its one empirical result bearing on the claim is a simulation (Figure 1): synthetic regression with d=32, n=1024, nnet/keras, sweeping neuron count. The authors say the blue MISE curve 'clearly exhibits this double descent' and that other regularization levels give other patterns. This is a new setting with a qualitative result on V1 and V6. The theorems bound tail error under path-norm regularization but cannot show a peak.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors prove that path-norm/weight-decay-regularized deep networks are statistically consistent for least-squares, Huber, quantile regression and classification, whatever the width. As size grows, approximation error falls while regularization keeps generalization error bounded, so the error curve's tail levels off at a non-zero constant. They add that growing networks past a threshold no longer reduces error, and that regularization strength changes whether the simulated curve shows double descent.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a synthetic regression simulation with nnet/Keras and MISE, plus path-norm regularization theory; it is not an explicit replication of the original experimental recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper states that different regularization levels can yield double descent or other patterns. The levels and their individual outcomes are not reported.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorems 1–2 give a prediction-error bound for path-norm-regularized deep ReLU networks. Approximation error falls with width while the regularized generalization error stays bounded, so tail error plateaus at a non-zero level rather than diverging.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under explicit norm regularization, test error of very large networks does not grow with size and converges to a constant set by generalization and optimization error.

record.problems: The simulation results are qualitative in the text, with no numerical values or uncertainty estimates reported. Package-specific outcomes and regularization-level mappings are not given. The interpolation threshold is not measured or located.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were omitted. Other consistency bounds for robust regression, quantile regression, classification, and random forests do not report the model-wise double-descent behavior at issue; cited findings are excluded.

untested.parts: Whether the peak sits near the size that just fits the training set. Training error and the interpolation threshold are not reported.
Label-noise dependence (noise fixed at 0.2), triple or multiple peaks, and disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
Not tested. Training ran long enough to avoid early stopping, and no epoch sweep is reported.
Not tested. There is no sample-size sweep.
Not tested. Random forests are analysed only as a theoretical bounded-variance argument, with no capacity curve.

missing.what: Numeric MISE values per neuron count, per package (nnet vs keras) and per regularization level; location of the peak in K relative to n=1024.

record.verdict_notes: The abstract describes double descent loosely as error decreasing monotonically to a constant; its focus is the tail, not the peak. The empirical evidence is a single illustrative figure described in two sentences, so all verdicts rest on the authors' qualitative wording. No noise variation, repeats or uncertainty are reported for the simulation.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not state whether the peak is near the model size that just fits the training set, or report the training-fit threshold.
No sweep over training epochs or training time is reported.
No sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold is reported.
The paper discusses double descent and random forests, but does not test a double-descent curve across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.

The paper varies regularization in its simulation and reports that curves can differ. It does not vary label noise, report triple or multiple peaks, or establish disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
No re-counting of complexity by an effective parameter measure is tested.

rows.uncertainty: With probability at least 1−O(n^−r), for large r.

rows.check: This is a theoretical upper bound on prediction error for large regularized networks, not a measured curve. A bound cannot show a fall-rise-fall shape or a peak, so 'partial' overstates what it shows. It only implies that error stays bounded as width grows.

statements.correction: Section 2, Theorem 2: prediction-error upper bound under hierarchical target assumptions and independent Gaussian residuals; prescribed penalty λn = c√(Lk ln²(n)/n); no reported regularization switch or confidence-driven removal of double descent. Section 1, Figure 1: qualitative double descent for the blue MISE curve; other patterns under different regularization levels; no measured interpolation threshold.
statements.problem: The simulation's regularization dependence and the distinction between bounds and measured risk are sound.
